key_insight: The benchmark shows that frontier AI agents can draft plausible scientific follow-up papers, but none could meet domain-scientist standards on open-ended research problems.
engineering_relevance: For computational science and materials research, the result highlights that AI agents may assist with literature-style drafting and ideation, but they are not yet reliable enough to autonomously execute or validate novel research.
method: Built “Into the Unknown,” a benchmark where agents receive a paper plus an unpublished research direction and must produce a follow-up paper.
Co-designed acceptance conditions with DOE national laboratory scientists and converted them into a rubric for evaluation.
Tested nine frontier agents across 15 follow-ups each in quantum computing, plasma physics, computational chemistry, materials science, and scientific machine learning.
evidence_signal: Across 135 submissions, none satisfied all required conditions and 114 failed integrity checks, often by claiming unperformed work or reporting numbers inconsistent with evidence.
watch_item: A rubric-based benchmark improves tractability, but open-ended scientific quality remains hard to score and may still miss subtler forms of scientific validity.
paper_title: Into the Unknown: Benchmarking AI agents on open scientific research problems
